Messages.Author: Herve Guillemet
Messages.Body:
What is the current rulling on Rotschreck ?

I know this issue has been intensively discussed, but the only ruling
I have seen states that it is the vampire dealing aggravated damage
that goes to torpor and :
- because of the reference by the name to the RPG,
- because of the drawing,
- because of the text,
- for the sake of game balance and logic,
I really think the card was designed to send the vampire about to
receive aggravated damages to torpor, before she can strike, and that it
should be played as such.

== Hervé Guillemet

Hmmm. This is very interesting, because it is my opinion that:

- because of the reference by the name to the RPG,

- for the sake of game balance and logic,

that the card should remain as ruled by the DTR.

I will concede that the text of the card does does read in favor of your
opinion, but the drawing is ambiguous, as there is no aggressor in the
piccture to indicate dealing aggravated damage, merely the presence of
potential aggravated damage. For all we know the vampire in the picture
opened the shades on himself (Burst of Sunlight). However, I refuse to
listen to this game definition of Rotchreck as justification for overruling
the DTR's decision. Rotchreck applies to any vampire ENCOUNTERING aggrivated
damage, not ATTACKED WITH aggravated damage. If you look in the Sabbat
Player's Guide, you'll notice that it says vampires have to be pretty
insane to use a flamethrower. This is because a vampire who isn't already
insane will be so after experiencing continuous jets of flame within an
arm's length of himself. So, basically, Vampire: the Masquerade does not
lend sympathy to your argument, particularly because the vampires who aren't
attempting to use aggravated damage are free to move away from it in a
rational manner. This leaves play balance. As you read the card, it
lends nothing to play balance. There is no effective counter for aggravated
damage, and it becomes even more impossible to avoid. Already a vampire
has to be able to dodge or prevent damage in order to avoid going to torpor,
and now you want to take away those options as well. Why do you want to
do this? Is your deck a Gangrel deck that can't cope with people building
decks that can do something other than Wolf Claws, something like Dodge,
maybe. Because we know dodge is too powerful a card. What we need is a
dodge hoser (because Immortal Grapple doesn't do that already)! Yes,
dodge is unbalanced, we need to restrict it even maybe. Is that what you
think? Because by your ruling that is basically what Rotchreck does.
It serves no other purpose than to cover up the inadiquacies of your
combat deck. As the DTR ruled it on the other hand, it becomes a useful
deterrent to aggravated damage cards that can torpor/burn vampires with
little or no effort. It is still very restricted in that it can't be
used on the player's turn, so it is only usable during a block (or Madness
Network). Do you seriously think that a card that can only be used while
blocking, can only be used against a minion dealing aggravated damage, and
costs a master phase action is unbalanced? Do you seriously think it is
better to have a card that bolsters the power of aggravated damage, which
can already torpor or burn any vampire without dodges or fortitude? If
you do, then I think you have serious problems with the concept of play
balance. Oh, by the way, if you find a group that agrees to your ruling,
I want to come over and play a Gangrel intercept deck :)

Messages.Author: Herve Guillemet
Messages.Body:
I (guil...@imed.jussieu.fr) wrote:

>- because of the reference by the name to the RPG,

>- because of the drawing,

>- because of the text,

>- for the sake of game balance and logic,

>I really think the card was designed to send the vampire about to
>receive aggravated damages to torpor, before she can strike, and that it
>should be played as such.

In fact, there are 2 issues:
- What the card was originally meant to do ?
and:
- What the card should do, to be the most in favor of the
Almighty Game Balance ?

The 2 issues could very well have 2 distinct answers and I agree that
the answer to the second one should prevail and determine the ruling.
However, if the answer to the second is not clear, the first one should
prevail.

What the card was meant to do ?
-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-
- The reference: Rotschek is the innate fright of vampires for the few
sources of damage that can really kill them. Particularly Fire and Sun.
One can think of it as an unintentional reaction of their organism to
avoid contact with those source and/or to avoid pain due to this contact.
Just like people faint just at the idea of something able to knock them
down. Thus it seems reasonable that Rotschek causes a vampire that knows
she will suffer AD to lose will and "faint" before she can strike himself
and actually suffers the AD.
MalKAViaN(naz...@wam.umd.edu) and Mage Bob
(Denni...@crpl.cedar-rapids.lib.ia.us) wrote that this phenomenon could
very well affect the vampire using AD. This is acceptable as long as the
AD are fire or sun but not claws, bow, dagger or pulled fang.
- The drawing: only confirms that the card deals with the fear of AD
- The text: it says, as David Gausebeck(gaus...@uiuc.edu) pointed it out:
Usable when a MINION inflicts aggravated damage to a VAMPIRE. That VAMPIRE
goes to torpor... So it's usable when a non-vampire minion, say a vampire
hunter wielding a flame thrower, fights a vampire. I can't see why, and
how, the vampire hunter will go to torpor. IMO the text is clear,
despite what Mage Bob(Denni...@crpl.cedar-rapids.lib.ia.us) wrote.

=> The card was meant to affect the vampire about to receive the damages.

What the card should do
-=-=-==-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=
In other words, is it better to hose the aggravated damages or to reinforce
them ? I don't think aggravated damages are too powerfull to need
a hoser, nor that the reinforcement this card allows is critical.
In most cases, the victim vampire will anyway go to torpor and the
Rotscheck only works as a damage prevention card as the victim will
not do her damage. And you know that a master card is a higher cost
that a combat card. In some case, where the victim could have
avoided the damage, the advantage Rotscheck grants IS critical. But this
happens when:
- the aggressor has in hand or control a card that inflicts AD
- the aggressor has Rotscheck in hand
- the victim has a dodge or a damage prevention card
So an efficacious Rotschek occurs at a frequency similar to a 3-card combo,
that is, seldom.
MalKAViaN and Mage Bob wrote this is a way to send vampire to torpor
you can do nothing against. They're right when the above opportunity
occurs, but you still can Sudden Reversal, as well as you can Sudden
Reversal a Golconda or a Hostile Takeover. Besides, as the Rotschek
necessarily happens during the victim turn, the vampire can usually
leave the dangerous torpor during the same turn.
There also the "can't untap at the next untap" effect, I admit this
one is probably too much.

A last, and not the least, reason I'll give, is that Rotschek, played the
other way, is a deck hoser. I hate deck hosers. It's always irritating to
play against a deck designed to counter your very deck. It incites
side-boards. And I think the possibility to build decks that works more or
less against some kinds of decks is the greater and the common flaw
of all trading-card games. In our play group, we banned clan hosers.
Rotschek, the way I suggest to play it, just integrates into a deck
strategy, and is not thrown into any kind of deck to counter a particular
strategy. I think this way to design deck is better for the "feeling"
of the game, even if it's not clearly better for its "balance".



There are others where it doesn't make sense for Rotschrek to affect the
aggressor, too. Claws of the Dead, obviously. Or Dragon Breath Rounds (at
least until after strike resolution) or Ivory Bow. Better yet, Basilia:
"It's... It's... MY HANDS!!! AAAAAAH!" Pulled Fangs. And more, I'm sure. In
any case, there are way too many to add to the card text.

And in every case it would be reasonable for Rotschrek to be inspired in the
victim. I think that logically it's much more reasonable for the victim to be
affected.

>>- because of the text,
>

>Read it again, over and over untill you get it right, remember improper
>nouns & punctuation...

I have read the text carefully, and I think the text is also (although not
overwhelmingly) in favor of the victim going to torpor (_minion_ attempts
against _vampire_, _vampire_ is put in torpor).

>
>>- for the sake of game balance and logic,

That's the problem. For game balance, Rotschrek should definitely affect the
minion attempting aggravated damage. The card seems fairly clearly to affect
the victim, but would be a much more reasonable card if it affected the
aggressor. I think they should stick with the current interpretation but call
it errata rather than a ruling.

-Dave Gausebeck

When there are hosers, you can't just play the `optimal' deck that
you like. Mathematically speaking, your optimal deck-building
strategy has to be a mixed strategy. In practical terms, you
have to build entirely distinct decks (not just making slight
modifications) and pull one out somehow randomly to play.

In a CCG, this has the obvious disadvantage of handicapping
players who don't have a $$$ large collection, and who don't
have cards to field multiple decks. Clan Hosers and strategy
hosers hose newbies above anybody else.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie

>When there are hosers, you can't just play the `optimal' deck that
>you like. Mathematically speaking, your optimal deck-building
>strategy has to be a mixed strategy. In practical terms, you
>have to build entirely distinct decks (not just making slight
>modifications) and pull one out somehow randomly to play.
>
>In a CCG, this has the obvious disadvantage of handicapping
>players who don't have a $$$ large collection, and who don't
>have cards to field multiple decks. Clan Hosers and strategy
>hosers hose newbies above anybody else.

If someone has just started playing, and yet people are ruining their
fun by hosing the best decks they can put together, then that person
can simply trade for another set of cards. Hosers are there to keep
people on their toes, and so that people won't simply zoom in on
the optimal strategy and focus on it. They are not there to address
issues that a new player is likely to be concerned with. For example,
its much more likely that an experienced player is going to be shut
down by a clan hoser like Cultivated Blood Shortage, if only because
they're more likely to be playing a monoclan deck.
